## Resume essentials

Note: I searched the web for "Northwind Analytics" and found no real company by that name operating in logistics/scheduling software in Phoenix — the posting itself says this is a fictional company built for a test fixture, so there is nothing to verify externally about it. All "facts" about the company below come only from the posting text you gave me, not from outside research.

The posting repeats a specific set of words — mirror them on your resume:

- **"Interview customers" / "analyse support tickets"** — Your internship answering customer calls and logging complaints for a moving company is direct evidence of this. Bullet it as something like: "Logged and categorized [X] customer complaint calls per week, surfacing [your top recurring issue] for management" — fill in the real numbers.
- **"Write user stories and acceptance criteria" / "keep the backlog prioritised"** — Your background doesn't show formal backlog work. Evidence that would show it: any time you turned a vague request into a written, ordered list of tasks — e.g., how you planned a PM Club event from idea to execution. Frame it that way rather than inventing product-management language you haven't used.
- **"Track product metrics ... report on them monthly"** — Your club attendance tracking (22 → 41 students average) and the Google Sheets sign-up tracker are good evidence of measuring and reporting a number over time. Bullet: "Built and maintained a Google Sheets tracker for club sign-ups; used it to grow average event attendance from 22 to 41 students across 5 events."
- **"Comfort with data: spreadsheets required, SQL a plus"** — Spreadsheets: covered by the tracker and the complaint log. SQL: you don't have it (see gaps below); don't claim it.
- **"Evidence of leading a project or team"** — Events chair of the PM Club for two semesters is exactly this. Lead with it, not bury it.
- **"Curiosity about logistics and supply chains"** — Your moving-company internship is logistics-adjacent; say so explicitly rather than assuming the reader will connect it.
- **Nice-to-haves (Jira, agile/scrum, product/consulting internship)** — Nothing in your background shows these. Evidence that would show it: a free Scrum/Agile fundamentals certificate, or using Jira/Trello for even a club project, before you apply.

## Handling your gaps

**No SQL.**
Honest framing: "I haven't used SQL yet, but I'm comfortable with the logic of filtering and aggregating data — I built a Sheets tracker for our club that did exactly that — and I'm actively learning SQL now." This is honest and confident because it names the real overlap (spreadsheet logic) instead of pretending the gap doesn't exist.
Concrete step before the interview: complete a free introductory SQL course (e.g., a few hours of a platform like Mode's SQL tutorial or Khan Academy) and be ready to say specifically what you learned, such as writing a `SELECT`/`WHERE`/`GROUP BY` query — [your specific example].

**Never worked in software.**
Honest framing: "I haven't worked inside a software company, but I've been the person translating a real-world problem — customer complaints, event logistics — into something a small team could act on, which is the core of this role." This works because it reframes the gap around the transferable skill (translating problems into action) rather than apologizing for the missing label.
Concrete step before the interview: read Northwind Analytics' "About us" and role description closely, then write down [one specific workflow or metric from the posting] you'd ask about — showing you can engage with a software product even without having worked in one.

## Questions to prepare for

- "Why product management, and why this role?" — Tests whether you understand what a PM actually does day to day, not just the title's appeal.
- "Tell me about a time you led a project or team." — Looks for your PM Club leadership story told with a clear problem, action, and measurable result (22 → 41 attendance).
- "How would you prioritize a backlog with limited engineering time?" — Checks whether you can reason about trade-offs, not whether you already know a specific framework.
- "Walk me through how you'd investigate a spike in customer complaints." — Directly mirrors "analyse support tickets" in the posting; shows whether you think in terms of data and root causes.
- "What would you track to know if a new feature is working?" — Tests fluency with the metrics named in the posting (adoption, retention, time-to-plan).
- "Tell me about a time you got conflicting feedback from two people and how you resolved it." — Looks for maturity in balancing stakeholders, relevant to coordinating with sales, customer success, and engineers.
- "What do you know about logistics or supply chains?" — Specific to this posting's emphasis on "curiosity about logistics"; shows whether you did any homework beyond the job description.

## Smart questions to ask

- "The posting mentions shipping improvements every two weeks — what does that cadence look like in practice, and how much of it is driven by the APM versus the senior PM?"
- "You've grown 40% a year for three years — what part of the route-planning product has had to change the most to keep up with that growth?" [unverified — this figure is from the posting, not independently confirmed]
- "How do you decide which customer interview findings turn into backlog items versus get set aside?"
- "What does the sales/customer success handoff look like when a release goes out?"
- "What's the biggest metric (adoption, retention, or time-to-plan) the team is currently trying to move, and why that one?"
- "What would success look like for whoever is in this seat after six months?"

## Summary

For Northwind Analytics' Associate Product Manager role (a fictional posting used as a test fixture), the strongest resume evidence is the PM Club leadership and attendance growth, the Google Sheets tracker, and the customer-complaint-logging internship — all of which map directly onto the posting's language about leadership, data, and customer interviews. The two real gaps, no SQL and no software-company experience, are best handled by naming the transferable skill honestly and completing one concrete prep step (a short SQL course, and close reading of the posting) before the interview.
